claims: Landing-control exercises must distinguish a non-jump drop, a jump or hop with flight, an elevated drop, and a run-to-stop because approach momentum and drop height change the task.
{{canonicalName}} must encode takeoff, landing laterality, direction, approach speed, external height, rebound intent, and required hold as identity, variant, or dosage dimensions.
Landing and horizontal deceleration both train force attenuation, but horizontal stopping additionally requires braking impulse to reduce whole-body momentum.
{{canonicalName}} belongs to landing and braking control; reactive rebounding, maximal jumping, change of direction, and conditioning are separate programming intents.
Force absorption is shared across the foot and ankle, knee, and hip rather than isolated to one joint.

The card should identify plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip abductors and external rotators, and trunk stabilizers with task-specific primary and secondary roles.
Effective braking coordinates lower-limb flexion, centre-of-mass control, foot placement, and force direction to attenuate and apply braking force.

Observable quality includes quiet controlled contact, whole-foot pressure, coordinated ankle-knee-hip flexion, knee tracking, stable pelvis and trunk, and ownership of the final position without extra steps.
Plyometric and landing intensity changes with speed, external height, body mass, external load, and task complexity.

Exercise difficulty must score technical complexity and physical demand directly, including coordination, impact, supervision, work capacity, and consequence of error; it must not use a skill-library level.
Horizontal deceleration creates high impact peaks, loading rates, and eccentric muscle demand; rapid or repeated exposures can contribute to muscle damage and need volume management.

{{canonicalName}} needs contact count, approach speed or drop height, laterality, eccentric braking demand, joint and tissue stress, performance-loss criteria, and recovery guidance rather than repetition count alone.
Landing interventions depend on appropriate materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a level non-slip surface, clear landing and run-out zones, stable equipment where applicable, suitable footwear, spacing, coach sightline, and a population-specific readiness screen.
Landing quality and force absorption should be learned before higher-speed, higher-height, repeated, or reactive plyometric work.
Prescribe low-repetition quality sets, landing contacts per side, approach speed or height, hold duration, rest, cue complexity, and progression criteria; stop before fatigue changes mechanics.
Prescriptive instructions and feedback can improve landing mechanics, while excessive or poorly targeted information can interfere with learning.
Use a small cue set: land quietly, share force through ankle-knee-hip flexion, keep knee over the middle toes, control pelvis and trunk, and hold the finish without a touch-down or extra step.
Loud contact, poor stabilization, loss of alignment, or inability to use the ankle, knee, and hip together indicate that intensity or volume exceeds current control.

Stop for pain, giving way, dizziness, repeated valgus or trunk collapse, uncontrolled foot contact, extra steps, loss of the required hold, unsafe surface or spacing, or persistent left-right asymmetry.
Landing stabilization and lower-body strength are recurring components of effective neuromuscular injury-prevention programs.

{{canonicalName}} belongs after general preparation and before high-intensity jumping, sprinting, or change-of-direction work; rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment require separate clinical context.
Athletes benefit from specific feedback tied to observable landing actions rather than abstract risk language.
Athlete support should show the start and finish positions, state the landing target and hold time, define a successful repetition, provide one primary cue, and explain the stop signal.
Coach education and practical implementation affect whether landing interventions can be delivered effectively.

Coach support should provide front and side observation points, pass-fail criteria, contact counting, left-right comparison, regressions, progressions, equipment checks, and rules for reducing speed, height, distance, or laterality.
Beginners should establish landing and stabilization control before progressing from bilateral to unilateral, longer, faster, or shock-loading tasks.

Accessibility can be improved with visual floor targets, demonstrated start and finish shapes, plain-language cues, reduced amplitude, external support, longer holds, and reduced sensory or decision load without assigning an exercise skill level.
In-place landings, jumps covering distance, repeated hops, and elevated or externally loaded tasks have different intensity and programming implications.

Direction, laterality, support, cueing, and low amplitude are usually variants; rebound intent, approach momentum, external height, or a change to testing or return-to-sport purpose may require a distinct definition or contextual profile.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The direct candidates for {{canonicalName}} were discovered or rechecked through visible YouTube search and public oEmbed metadata; full viewing, exact-version match, captions, instructional quality, safety, and approval remain pending human review.

assessmentSummary.identity: A low-speed horizontal braking drill: take one purposeful step into a marked stop position, lower the centre of mass, and hold the final stance without an extra recovery step.
currentCardFindings: The legacy title is misleading: this is not a step-down strength exercise and it does not require stepping from a box.
The legacy execution describes a forward, diagonal, or lateral stop step with a two-second hold, making approach direction a delivery variant rather than a separate card.
Controlled taxonomy, anatomy, load, fatigue, environment, and population fields are empty; the name collision with strength step-downs also produces irrelevant media matches.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the athlete reaches the target with one braking step and owns every hold without trunk collapse or foot shuffle

coachCues: Step to the marker and sink into the stop
Keep pressure through the whole foot
Knee follows the middle toes
Freeze without another step
athleteInstructions: Take one controlled step into the target
Lower your hips as the foot contacts
Hold the finish for two seconds
commonFaults: reaching too far with the foot
confusing the drill with a box step-down

readiness: pain-free walking lunge or split stance
stopRules: cannot stop within the marked zone

assessmentSummary.identity: An elevated mixed-vector landing drill intended to combine a controlled box step-off with a lateral displacement and a non-reactive final stick; the exact sequence remains quarantined because the legacy card does not state whether the lateral motion occurs during the drop or after an initial landing.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card conflates drop absorption, lateral ownership, and immediate reacceleration, which are different stimuli and should not share one definition.

The title can mean either a lateral box drop directly to the ground or a vertical depth drop followed by a lateral bound; the card does not specify the takeoff, intermediate contact, or landing laterality.
The controlled fields are empty and the current media pool contains both interpretations, so publication must wait for an identity decision.

assessmentSummary.identity: A unilateral non-jump landing-position drill: rapidly lower from tall single-leg stance into a controlled single-leg athletic position and hold without hopping or touching the free foot down.
currentCardFindings: The stable movement is a unilateral snap-down and stick, not a cut, sprint stop, or reacceleration drill as implied by generic legacy copy.
The task creates no intentional flight phase; it trains rapid position acquisition, single-leg balance, and eccentric control before hopping progressions.
Controlled taxonomy, anatomy, load, fatigue, environment, and population fields are empty, and the legacy media pool includes bilateral and snap-down-to-jump mismatches.
